title: Inference round-up: long-context caching, quantization tradeoffs, and lightweight eval ideas
summary: A messy personal roundup of recent papers and threads I want to check for the long-context workstream: focused notes on prefix/KV caching patterns that seem promising for our multi-tenant hosted API, quantization caveats that show up in instruction-following tasks, and a few lightweight eval ideas to catch regressions quickly.
content:
Quick brain dump (June sprint context):

— motivation: customers want 32k+ effective context with predictable latency; we can’t always increase KV cache size without hurting tail latency. need smarter eviction/prefetch and cheap on-the-fly compression.

Papers / threads I skimmed (high level):
  * adaptive prefix selection (paper X): idea = keep short summary vectors for old prefixes, only expand to full KV when score passes threshold. pretty attractive for cold starts.
  * kv compression via quantized residuals (blog Y): store 8-bit base + few-bit residuals for older tokens; does fine for retrieval-heavy prompts but hurts generative diversity.
  * prompt chunking + stitched attention (ICLR workshop notes): split into segments, compute local contexts then cross-attend with small global tokens — reduces memory by ~30% on benchmarks.

Experiment notes I want to run: (rough)
  - baseline: 8xA100 serving with naive KV cache (no compression), sequence length distribution sampled from hosted logs (median 2048, 95th 18k). measure p50/p95/p99 latency for generations up to 4k tokens.
  - trial A: apply 4-bit asymmetric quantization on stored KV (per-token scale + offset, per-head?) — test for perplexity gap and generation quality on instruction-following prompts (use eval set X).
  - trial B: prefix-summarizer: run lightweight encoder (2-layer transformer) to produce 256-d summary per 2k tokens; store summary index and only decode full KV when similarity>theta. measure hit-rate and cost.
  - trial C: LRU vs recency+salience eviction using attention-energy score.

Early hypotheses / expectations:
  - 4-bit per-token KV will reduce memory 2x but may leak fine-grained identity signals required for code generation and math -> failure modes mainly in chain-of-thought tasks.
  - prefix-summarizer will save memory for long-lived sessions where user appends lots of non-informative context (e.g., chat history), but hurts steps that require exact token recall (e.g., citations).

Evaluation ideas (lightweight monitors to catch quality regressions):
  1) fingerprint prompts: small set (~200) of diagnostic prompts split across genres (code, math, QA, dialog). Run nightly with new serving config; compute delta on logits and generate BLEU/ROUGE/LLM-eval style checks.
  2) token-diff heatmap: instrument served requests to capture positions where quantized-KV vs baseline produce top-1 token changes; focus on early divergence positions (first 50 tokens).
  3) rollout canary: route 1% traffic to quantized-KV variant, keep offline evals + small user-sentinel set (internal redwood-sentinel workspace) to manually spot hallucination patterns.

Scratch notes / heuristics gleaned so far (informal):
  - if you see tokens that are dense and repeat (json blobs, logs) you can compress aggressively. natural text -> be conservative.
  - per-head quant scales matter: mixing per-head vs per-layer changes the SNR distribution; per-head seems more consistent but more metadata to store.
  - precompute attention-energy distribution for early eviction decisions (cheap scalar per token) — seems to correlate with future reuse.

Unresolved questions / open experiments:
  - what is the right threshold for prefix-summarizer similarity? (0.7??) needs calibration per workload.
  - how to roll quantized-kv to dedicated customers with SLAs? probably staged: offline eval -> canary -> opt-in config flag.
  - eviction fairness across tenants: one noisy tenant shouldn’t push other's KV out — maybe per-tenant quotas + shared pool.

Useful snippets / commands: (for myself later)
  - synthetic workload generator: python tools/generate_ctx_workload.py --log-sample hosted_logs.parquet --target-dist "mix(0.6:short,0.3:mid,0.1:long)" --out synthetic_ctx_2028-06.json
  - perf profile: perf record -F 99 -g -- ./serve_bin --model x --kv-mode quantized --batching=continuous

Notes-to-self: link concrete numbers in next doc: memory/disk cost per 1M tokens of kv at 8-bit vs 4-bit vs compressed-residual. also quantify extra CPU to dequantize per token.

Meeting followups (people to ping):
  - @Maya: ask for the hosted-logs sample for June 2028 range (need latency buckets + sequence lengths).
  - @Omar: get initial perf counters from recent dedicated run (June 6) where we saw a weird RPC serialization spike.
  - infra SRE: sanity check on eviction-induced tail latency when cache churn spikes.

Rough timeline for next week:
  - Mon: pick baseline config and run synthetic workload (measure memory and tail latencies)
  - Wed: implement per-head 4-bit kv serialization in toy runtime (local)
  - Fri: small offline eval on diagnostic prompt set, prepare canary config if numbers look okay.

Closing messy thought: we should try a hybrid: aggressive compression for tokens older than T minutes + preserve last N tokens verbatim. This seems operationally simple and might buy most wins without complicated summarizers.

End of dump.
takeaways: Aggressive KV compression buys memory but risks failures on precise tasks (code/math)
Lightweight summarization can reduce memory for chat-heavy sessions, but requires calibrated similarity thresholds
Need automated, small diagnostic suite to detect quality regressions early when changing KV storage or eviction
